Within the incoming Democratic majority in the U.S. House of Representatives,
lawmakers are hotly debating a potentially massive, Donald Trump-shaped hole
in the middle of one of their Day 1 congressional priorities following the
GOP's 2026 "[bloodbath](https://zeteo.com/p/republicans-groan-trump-and-
stephen)."

Knowledgeable sources, including elected Dems and senior staffers on Capitol
Hill, tell **Zeteo** that as Democratic lawmakers and their aides prepare to
introduce comprehensive federal legislation banning stock trading by members
of Congress, Supreme Court justices, senior administration officials, spouses,
and others, divisions have already opened up in the caucus over one key detail
of how they write the bill. The question being: _Should we even include the
president of the United States?_

On Day 1 of the new Congress, Democrats can make a House rule banning
congressional stock trading; liberals campaigned on doing this during the
midterm elections, as these trades are - for good reason - widely viewed as a
form of elite corruption with obvious potential for insider trading. But that
rule wouldn't be a law, and various legislators and nonprofit groups are
pushing to pass new legislation to stop government personnel and elected
officials from directly profiting off of companies for which U.S. policy
decisions could easily sink or boost their stocks.

But as Democratic lawmakers will flatly tell you: There is _no way on Earth_
that President Trump - who has [traded more
securities](https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2026-trump-stock-trades-
congress/), since he reclaimed office, than every member of Congress combined,
and whose family business empire is making a gargantuan fortune - will sign a
ban that applies to him and his office.

As Democratic congresspeople consider a stock-trading ban next year, they have
broken off primarily into three categories.
